justification_text:
At the time of the forecast, the asset appeared to be trading near the 1000 level, and my point estimates reflect a broadly neutral to very slightly bullish drift over time. For the 1-day estimate of 998, I was essentially anchoring close to the prevailing price with minimal expected movement, consistent with mean-reversion tendencies over very short horizons. The 1-week estimate of 1002 incorporates a small positive drift, reflecting the general long-run upward bias seen in many financial assets while acknowledging that one week is still a short window where noise dominates. The 1-month estimate of 1010 extends that modest drift further, implying roughly a 1% expected gain over the month, which aligns with typical annualized return assumptions scaled down to a monthly horizon.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, a range of roughly plus or minus 28 points around the estimate reflects typical daily volatility, which for many equity indices or similar instruments runs in the 1–3% range. By one week, the interval widens to about plus or minus 52 points, consistent with volatility scaling by the square root of time. At one month, the interval expands to roughly plus or minus 100 points, capturing the full breadth of plausible outcomes when macro data, earnings, and sentiment shifts have time to play out.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden geopolitical shock, an unexpected central bank policy announcement, or a sharp deterioration in credit or liquidity conditions could easily breach the lower bounds, particularly at the 1-month horizon. A major inflation surprise or a financial contagion event could produce moves of 15–20% or more, far outside the stated range. On the upside, an unexpected policy pivot toward easing, a strong batch of economic data, or a short-squeeze dynamic in a positioning-heavy market could drive prices well above the upper bounds.

It is also worth acknowledging that these intervals represent 90% confidence bounds, meaning roughly one in ten outcomes is expected to fall outside them even under normal conditions. Fat-tailed distributions, which are common in financial markets, mean the true probability of extreme outcomes is likely higher than a normal distribution would imply. Regime changes — such as a transition from a low-volatility environment to a high-volatility one — are particularly difficult to anticipate and can render even well-constructed intervals obsolete quickly.
